The 30 Best WNBA Players of All Time, Ranked

A’ja Wilson, Maya Moore, Breanna Stewart, and Diana Taurasi are among the WNBA’s 30 best players through 30 seasons.

By Thomas Golianopoulos, Bryanna Symone, Jeff Smith
July 23, 2026
Re-Rank
Photo by Gina Ferazzi/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images; Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images; Photo by Harry How/Getty Images; Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images

Thirty seasons in, the WNBA has built a history deep enough to argue about. The league that tipped off in 1997 with eight teams now fills arenas, moves merchandise, and produces generational talent at a rate its founders could only have hoped for. So who sits at the very top of it? The all-time leading scorer, Diana Taurasi? The player who walked away in her prime, Maya Moore? The best player alive right now, A’ja Wilson? Or a champion from the very first era, like Cynthia Cooper?

This list covers every era of the league — the pioneers who pulled on a jersey in 1997, the stars who carried the WNBA through its lean years, and the players redefining it today. Ranking across thirty seasons means weighing eras that barely resemble each other.

We weighed peak dominance, longevity, championships, individual hardware, and the mark each player left on the sport beyond the box score. Reasonable people will disagree, which is rather the point. Here is our ranking of the 30 Best WNBA Players of All Time, Ranked.

30
Paige Bueckers
Photo by Sam Hodde/Getty Images
Seasons: 2025–Present
Accolades: 2025 Rookie of the Year

The newest name here, and the one most likely to climb. Bueckers arrived in Dallas as the most hyped guard of her draft class and immediately looked the part, running an offense with the poise of a veteran. Her placement is a bet on what comes next rather than a verdict on what she has already done — which is exactly why she is a lightning rod for this list. —TG
29
Chamique Holdsclaw
Doug Pensinger /Allsport
Seasons: 1999–2007
Accolades: 1999 Rookie of the Year, 6x All-Star

For a stretch around the turn of the century, Holdsclaw was the most gifted forward in the league. She came out of Tennessee as the most decorated college player in the country and translated it immediately, scoring from everywhere with a fluid, unhurried game. Injuries and time away shortened the peak, but at her best she was untouchable. —TG
28
DeWanna Bonner
Photo by Elsa/Getty Images
Seasons: 2009–Present
Accolades: 2x WNBA Champion, 6x All-Star, All-Time Top-5 Scorer

Longevity is its own kind of greatness, and Bonner has more of it than almost anyone. She won twice early in Phoenix as a scorer off the bench, then reinvented herself as a full-time starter and climbed the all-time scoring list season after season. Few players have stayed this productive for this long. —BS
27
Chelsea Gray
Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images
Seasons: 2015–Present
Accolades: 2x WNBA Champion, 2022 Finals MVP, 6x All-Star

Nicknamed the Point Gawd, and the nickname is earned. Gray is the guard you want when a possession has gone sideways and someone has to invent a shot. Her 2022 postseason run in Las Vegas was one of the great playoff performances by a guard, a stretch where she simply could not be guarded. —BS
26
Jonquel Jones
Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images
Seasons: 2016–Present
Accolades: 2021 MVP, WNBA Champion, Finals MVP

A 6-foot-6 forward who shoots from the perimeter and rebounds like a center, Jones is the kind of player the modern game was built to accommodate. She won MVP in Connecticut, then delivered a title in New York, showing she could be the best player on a championship team rather than merely a very good one. —JS
25
Deanna Nolan
Photo by Jed Jacobsohn/Getty Images
Seasons: 2001–2009
Accolades: 3x WNBA Champion, 2006 Finals MVP, 5x All-Star

Tweety Nolan was the engine of the Detroit Shock dynasty, a two-way guard who defended the opponent's best scorer and then went and got 20 herself. She retired early and by her own choice, which has kept her out of some conversations she belongs in. —TG
24
Katie Smith
Photo by Domenic Centofanti/Getty Images
Seasons: 1999–2013
Accolades: WNBA Champion, 7x All-Star, Naismith Hall of Fame

One of the most reliable scorers of her generation and a genuinely great three-point shooter before that was standard. Smith carried offenses in Minnesota, won late in her career in Detroit, and left with a Hall of Fame case built on consistency rather than any single spectacular season. —JS
23
Angel McCoughtry
Photo by Tim Clayton/Corbis via Getty Images
Seasons: 2009–2022
Accolades: 2x Scoring Champion, 5x All-Star

McCoughtry attacked relentlessly and drew fouls at a rate that made her nearly impossible to defend cleanly. She led the league in scoring twice and took Atlanta to multiple Finals, falling short of a title but never short of effort. —BS
22
Cappie Pondexter
Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images
Seasons: 2006–2018
Accolades: 2x WNBA Champion, 2007 Finals MVP, 7x All-Star

A pure scorer with the temperament for big moments. Pondexter won two titles in Phoenix, took Finals MVP in the first, and later became the centerpiece in New York. When a game needed a shot made, she was the one who made it. —TG
21
Lindsay Whalen
Photo by Hannah Foslien/Getty Images
Seasons: 2004–2018
Accolades: 4x WNBA Champion, 5x All-Star, Naismith Hall of Fame

Whalen was the floor general of the Minnesota dynasty, a guard whose toughness and vision set the tone for four championship teams. She was never the leading scorer and never needed to be — she made everyone around her better and won more than almost anyone. —JS
20
Napheesa Collier
Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images)
Seasons: 2019–Present
Accolades: 2024 Defensive Player of the Year, 2019 Rookie of the Year

Collier does everything at a high level and nothing wastefully. She defends multiple positions, scores efficiently inside and out, and has been in the MVP conversation while anchoring Minnesota's defense. A model of the modern two-way forward. —BS
19
Brittney Griner
Photo by Jonathan Daniel/Getty Images
Seasons: 2013–Present
Accolades: WNBA Champion, 2x Defensive Player of the Year, 9x All-Star

Griner changed how teams had to think about the paint. At her peak she was the most intimidating rim protector the league had seen, blocking shots at historic rates while scoring efficiently on the other end. The 2014 title in Phoenix is the crown on it. —TG
18
Tina Charles
Photo by Matthew Grimes Jr./Getty Images
Seasons: 2010–Present
Accolades: 2012 MVP, 2010 Rookie of the Year, 8x All-Star

A relentless rebounder and a consistent post scorer across more than a decade. Charles won MVP in Connecticut and has stayed productive across several franchises since, quietly assembling one of the great statistical careers in league history. —JS
17
Sue Bird
Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images
Seasons: 2002–2022
Accolades: 4x WNBA Champion, All-Time Assists Leader, 13x All-Star

Twenty seasons, one franchise, four championships, and more assists than anyone who has ever played. Bird's longevity is remarkable enough on its own, but it is the winning that settles it — Seattle was a contender for essentially her entire career. —BS
16
Seimone Augustus
Photo by Hannah Foslien/Getty Images
Seasons: 2006–2020
Accolades: 4x WNBA Champion, 2011 Finals MVP, 8x All-Star

The smoothest mid-range game of her era. Augustus was Minnesota's leading scorer at the start of its dynasty and remained its most efficient shot-maker throughout, a player who never seemed to force anything and rarely missed. —TG
15
Elena Della Donne
Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images
Seasons: 2013–2023
Accolades: 2x MVP, WNBA Champion, 2013 Rookie of the Year

At 6-foot-5 with a guard's shooting stroke, Delle Donne was a matchup nobody solved. She won two MVPs and delivered a championship to Washington in 2019, the same season she shot 50/40/90 — a mark of pure scoring skill almost nobody reaches. —JS
14
Tina Thompson
Photo by Karen Warren/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images
Seasons: 1997–2013
Accolades: 4x WNBA Champion, 9x All-Star, Naismith Hall of Fame

The very first pick in WNBA history, and a foundational figure in every sense. Thompson won four titles with Houston, retired as the league's all-time leading scorer, and stretched her game to the three-point line before that was expected of a forward. —BS
13
Nneka Ogwumike
Photo by Harry How/Getty Images
Seasons: 2012–Present
Accolades: 2016 MVP, WNBA Champion, 2012 Rookie of the Year

Ogwumike's 2016 was close to a perfect season — MVP, a championship, and shooting numbers that looked like a misprint. Beyond the honours she has been among the league's most consequential voices on how players are treated and paid. —TG
12
Yolanda Griffith
Photo by Jed Jacobsohn/Getty Images
Seasons: 1999–2009
Accolades: 1999 MVP and Defensive Player of the Year, WNBA Champion

Griffith arrived in the league already fully formed and won MVP and Defensive Player of the Year in the same season. She was a ferocious rebounder and the defensive anchor of the Sacramento team that won it all in 2005. —JS
11
Lauren Jackson
Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images
Seasons: 2001–2012
Accolades: 3x MVP, 2x WNBA Champion, 7x All-Star

Perhaps the most skilled big the league has ever had. Jackson could score from the post, the mid-range, or beyond the arc, and won three MVPs doing it. Injuries cut the career short; the peak was as high as anyone's. —BS
10
Sheryl Swoopes
hoto by Otto Greule Jr/Getty Images
Seasons: 1997–2011
Accolades: 3x MVP, 4x WNBA Champion, 3x Defensive Player of the Year

Swoopes was the league's first signing and one of its first true two-way superstars — three MVPs, three Defensive Player of the Year awards, and four championships in Houston. A player who could win a game at either end. —TG
9
Lisa Leslie
Photo by Todd Warshaw/Allsport/Getty Images
Seasons: 1997–2009
Accolades: 3x MVP, 2x WNBA Champion, 2001 Finals MVP

For the league's first decade Leslie was its most recognisable player and its most dominant center. She won three MVPs, back-to-back titles in Los Angeles, and became the first player to dunk in a WNBA game — a moment that did as much for the league's profile as any. —JS
8
Sylvia Fowles
Photo by David Berding/Getty Images
Seasons: 2008–2022
Accolades: 2017 MVP, 2x WNBA Champion, 4x Defensive Player of the Year

Fowles retired as the league's all-time leading rebounder, which undersells how complete she was. Four Defensive Player of the Year awards, an MVP, two titles in Minnesota, and a career of astonishing efficiency around the basket. —BS
7
Candace Parker
Photo by Leon Bennett/Getty Images
Seasons: 2008–2023
Accolades: 2x MVP, 3x WNBA Champion, 2008 Rookie of the Year

Parker won Rookie of the Year and MVP in the same season, which had never been done, then spent fifteen years proving it was no fluke. She won titles with three different franchises, the last of them in Las Vegas, and did it as a passer and defender as much as a scorer. —TG
6
Breanna Stewart
Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images
Seasons: 2016–Present
Accolades: 2x MVP, 3x WNBA Champion, 2016 Rookie of the Year

Stewart has won at every level she has played, and in the WNBA she has been the best player on championship teams in two different cities. A 6-foot-4 forward who shoots, passes, defends and rebounds, she has no obvious weakness to attack. —JS
5
Cynthia Cooper
Photo by Smiley N. Pool/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images
Seasons: 1997–2000, 2003
Accolades: 2x MVP, 4x WNBA Champion, 4x Finals MVP

Nobody has ever owned a run of seasons like Cooper owned the league's first four. Four championships, four Finals MVPs, two league MVPs — an unbroken stretch of dominance that no one has come close to repeating. The career was short, which is the only argument against her. —BS
4
Maya Moore
Photo by Tim Clayton/Corbis via Getty Images
Seasons: 2011–2018
Accolades: 2014 MVP, 4x WNBA Champion, 2011 Rookie of the Year

At her peak Moore was the most complete player in the world — four titles, an MVP, and a closing instinct that decided playoff games. Then she stepped away at 29 to fight for a man's freedom and won that too, which is why she is remembered as more than a basketball player. —TG
3
Tamika Catchings
Photo by Leon Bennett/Getty Images
Seasons: 2002–2016
Accolades: 2011 MVP, WNBA Champion, 5x Defensive Player of the Year

Catchings played fifteen seasons at a level of intensity most players cannot sustain for one. Five Defensive Player of the Year awards, an MVP, and a championship in Indiana, built on a motor that never idled. —JS
2
Diana Taurasi
Photo by Chris Coduto/Getty Images
Seasons: 2004–2024
Accolades: All-Time Leading Scorer, 2009 MVP, 3x WNBA Champion

Twenty seasons in Phoenix and more points than anyone who has ever played. Taurasi combined range, arrogance and durability into the most sustained scoring career in league history, and won three championships along the way. If the criterion is total career output, she is first. —BS
1
A’ja Wilson
Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images
Seasons: 2018–Present
Accolades: 3x MVP, 2x WNBA Champion, 2018 Rookie of the Year, 2x DPOY

Wilson is the best player in the world and has been for several years running — multiple MVPs, multiple championships, Defensive Player of the Year honours, and a single-season scoring record that reset expectations. She scores, defends and rebounds at an elite level simultaneously, and she is not finished. —TG
